scenarios.prompt: User hands over a 60-page team Java style guide and asks to 'just convert it into a skill, keep everything'.
expected: refuses verbatim conversion: builds the ownership mapping table first
keeps only language-level rules; generic clean-code items become a reference, process rules are redirected
prioritizes high-frequency high-risk rules into SKILL.md and moves the long tail to references/

scenarios.prompt: The team document mixes 'functions should be short', 'never block in interrupt context', and 'Java streams must not be used in hot loops'.
expected: classifies 'functions short' as generic clean-code (referenced, not duplicated)
classifies the interrupt rule as domain (embedded-development), not language
keeps only the Java-specific rule in java-coding-standards with a rationale and example

scenarios.prompt: The team Python document says nothing about mutable default arguments; the agent wants to silently add a strict rule as if the team required it.
expected: may propose the rule but labels it as a DevFlow default suggestion pending team confirmation
does not present invented rules as team mandates
lists document gaps for the standards owner to decide

scenarios.prompt: The team standard allows a macro pattern that devflow-clean-code discourages; the agent plans to drop the team rule.
expected: team rules take precedence over DevFlow defaults
records the conflict explicitly in the generated skill ('team convention, overrides DevFlow default')
raises the disagreement to the standards owner instead of silently rewriting

scenarios.prompt: The draft skill contains 'use appropriate exception handling' and a section with only a rules table and no code.
expected: rejects undecidable wording and rewrites it as a judgeable rule
requires a good/bad code pair in the target language for each topic section
checks the contract acceptance list before delivery
